extracted.intended_audience: bookbinders, printers, typographers, librarians, and informed readers interested in book design, preservation, and readable typography
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic guidelines for bookbinding, display/preservation (especially parchment), selection of important books, and empirical principles for printing and type-legibility to guide printers and designers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Decorative treatment of book covers should be 'flat ornament' rather than pictorial or perspectival work that invades the third dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use blind tooling, gilding, inlaying, surface rubbing (crushed levant, tree or marbled calf effects) and tooling forms with taste and skill. Avoid pictorial scenes or perspective on covers (these create an illusion of depth that is dispelled on opening). Embossing is a mild exception but should be used sparingly; heavy medieval ornamentation (studs, jewels) is out of fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every additional stroke must add beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: There is practically no limit to ornamenting a binding provided every additional stroke is an additional beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the binder lacks mastery, stop at simple lettering and avoid overworking the cover. Examples: minute ornament like Mearne vs few significant lines like Aldus or Roger Payne — treatment, not quantity, determines success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid invasion of painter/draftsman province
rubrics_metrics.description: Binders should not attempt pictorial or perspectival illusion on covers, which belongs to painters or draftsmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't produce cover scenes in perspective (analogy: one does not want to walk over a rug showing a perspective scene). Embossing is acceptable only when its intrusion into depth is slight and does not 'cheat the eye.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Design must respect material and production conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The best design is one that 'triumphs within the conditions, not outside them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different materials (leather vs cloth) and production methods (hand vs machine/edition work) impose different rules; in cloth (machine-made, edition work) ornament rules may be relaxed, but the decorative problem remains essentially the same—design should succeed given the material and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit machine-era overreach; value craft skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanization and division of labour have changed binding; masters of all processes are fewer and crafts suffer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits imposed by machine production and preserve craft excellence where possible; encourage renaissance of the hand craft despite economic pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parchment binding for long-term aesthetic value
rubrics_metrics.description: Parchment bindings gain value and beauty with age; they 'convert time into gold' and develop a rich tint prized by collectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parchment for books intended to gather mellowing beauty over centuries. The material tolerates dust and smudges by converting them into attractive tone. Consider binding annually the best contemporary books on durable papers in parchment for future value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display and preservation policy for antique parchments
rubrics_metrics.description: Century-mellowed parchments are precious and should be displayed with care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer open cases for display so all may enjoy them, but protect them from careless eyes; store them until a discerning reader requests them. Avoid leaving them hidden permanently; rotate display in controlled conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Librarian duty: create future heirlooms
rubrics_metrics.description: Librarians should select well-printed contemporary books on time-proof paper and have them bound in parchment annually to accumulate value for successors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is proposed as a service to future generations—choose annually the best books and bind them suitably for longevity and mellowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize 'the few great books' in a crowded publishing world
rubrics_metrics.description: Given enormous modern book output, readers must choose; the individual book remains an address from one mind to another, but time is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize reading by priorities: intellectual tools (profession-specific), general information (to be a contemporary citizen), and the best literature. Use lists of the best books (top 10/50/100) as practical guides; the will to read the best is the main requirement—the rest is curated for you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read profession-specific literature first (intellectual tools)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every profession or handicraft has its necessary literature which must be read as the first priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that some reading is 'bread and butter' (technical journals, manuals) and while not 'literature' they are essential; they occupy time that might otherwise be for 'books that are books.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Read for general information to remain a contemporary
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should include works that keep them informed about current affairs and knowledge to be 'men among the men of our time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes compends, reviews, and newspapers—necessary distractions that enlarge the reader's acquaintance with the world; balance with other reading aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include recreational reading judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Recreational literature (novels, humor) has a legitimate place and may broaden sympathies or refresh the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overindulge (e.g., a novel a day is a perversion of appetite), but allow a judicious proportion of fiction among heavier reading; some novels rank among the best books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt modest, persistent daily reading (e.g., 10 pages/day)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistent small daily reading accumulates substantial knowledge over years—Mathews' example: 10 pages/day (omitting Sundays) yields 3,130 pages/year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over five or more years this produces dozens of well-chosen volumes worth more than a typical collegiate education if well read and digested; persistence and selection matter more than genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scientific/quantitative testing to settle printing utility questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Printing matters (legibility, paper, ink, type forms) should be resolved by psychological and quantitative experiments rather than prejudice or opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science can measure the percentage superiority of competing choices; this quantitative knowledge helps balance aesthetic vs economic tradeoffs and predicts gains in reduced eye strain and time saving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper finish and color: test empirically
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface finish (eggshell, glaze, plate finishes) and paper color influence legibility and eye comfort and require comparative testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common opinion that eggshell or glaze hinders reading should be tested to see which is worse and by what degree; likewise test antique vs medium plate finishes, and different paper tints (buff, white, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ink/paper contrast and color selection affect readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between paper and ink is necessary, but the strongest contrast may not always be best; combinations (black on white, blue-black on buff-white, white on black) need empirical evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to counterintuitive results; quantitative tests should determine optimal contrast for legibility and eye comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine ideal line length, type size, and leading empirically
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions such as normal line length, ideal type size for different ages, and the effect of leading on legibility need experimental determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether newspapers' line lengths or books' type sizes are correct; assess whether each size of type has a normal line length and how leading interacts. Recognize that in poetic or reference works some legibility may be sacrificed for beauty or economy—measure how much.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type design variables to evaluate: weight, shading, condensation, extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether light or heavy, even or shaded, condensed or extended letters are more legible and in what proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from traditional forms (e.g., Caslon) but test which commercial types meet legibility conditions; identify potential modifications to improve poor letters and know when traditional forms reach limits and need new forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform specific letter shapes to improve legibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Some letters are inherently harder to recognize and should be modified (e.g., shorten overhang of 'a', slant bar of 'e', consider dropping dot of 'i', introduce new form of 'l').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target letters shown by experiments to be least legible (e.g., E, s, g, c, x). Since lowercase letters evolved later, they may be altered without sacrilege; small changes (shortenings, slants) or near-new forms may be warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shading and ornamental features in letterforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Shaded or ornamented type was found to be a disadvantage for legibility and a source of confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer fairly black types with uniform line thickness; condemn ornament and shading as hindrances to eye recognition (Cattell, Javal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider spacing (letters, words, paragraphs) as an alternative to punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Spacing — between letters, between words, and between paragraphs — can improve clarity and can in some cases supplement or replace punctuation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Javal favored spacing between letters; Cattell proposed supplementing or displacing punctuation with spaces corresponding to pauses. Evaluate spacing practices empirically for readability gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixed case where unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing capitals and small letters offers no clear legibility advantage according to experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cattell saw no benefit in a mixture of capitals and small letters; keep case use consistent unless tests show an advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize empirical letter-legibility order and its implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental orders of letter legibility show wide variation (e.g., Cattell: W recognized far more reliably than E; Sanford and others produced ranking orders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay special attention to the legibility of the most frequently used letters (e, t, a, i, n, o, s were near the bottom in some tests), since poor visibility of common letters wastes time and strains eye and brain; prioritize these letters in reform efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principles for improving letter legibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that aid legibility include enlargement, increase of differences between letters, simplicity of outline, and concentrating peculiarity on one distinguishing feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even small letters can be made highly legible by combining simplicity and a single distinctive feature (example: 'v' brought into first group by these qualities). Apply these principles when redesigning problematic letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation visibility concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuation marks are often hard to see and may interfere with legibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider displacing or supplementing punctuation with spacing conventions that reflect pauses in thought; test such changes for readability before adoption.
